book_growth.why: Year 1 growth is held down by the $64 million unrealized loss on bonds and by buybacks and dividends: nine-month equity growth was only about 4.5%, and I assume Q4 earnings lift the year to about 9%. long_run_roe.why: The company's niche underwriting and diversification support returns above the 9.3% cost of equity, but competition and softer pricing cycles should pull the return toward the mid-teens. Cat-exposed and reinsurance-dependent specialty insurers rarely hold ROEs above 20% indefinitely.

quotes.quote: Return on opening common equity over the years above: min 0.1261, p25 0.1324, median 0.2058, p75 0.2495, max 0.2703, last 0.2703.

roe.why: Nine-month 2026 ROE of 22.3% is below 2025's 23.6% (annual) and the underlying loss ratio is rising, so I expect year 1 near 23.5% and then a gradual fade as margins normalize, catastrophe losses revert toward their average, and interest and intangible amortization weigh on earnings. The record shows 2025's 27.0% on opening equity was a peak.

terminal_growth.why: A mature specialty insurer's book equity should grow roughly with nominal premium growth, slightly above the long-run anchor, given the company's still-expanding addressable market against a $1 trillion U.S. P&C market. I set it slightly below the anchor of 0.0375.

risks.risk: Attritional loss ratio keeps rising with the shift to Crop and Casualty, or reserves prove inadequate, compressing underwriting margins.
Severe catastrophe or reinsurance-market hardening and competition push long-run returns down towards the cost of equity.
Further bond mark-to-market losses, debt service, acquisition integration problems or ratings pressure slow equity accumulation.

situation.base_year_note: 2025 ROE of 0.2703 is above the 2026 run-rate.
situation.roe_position: Return on opening equity has risen from 12.6% in 2021 to 27.0% in 2025. The drivers were rapid premium growth, a retained share of premium that rose as cession percentages fell, and very light catastrophe losses (a catastrophe loss ratio of -0.1% in 2025). In 2026 the loss ratio rose sharply (Q3 41.5% against 32.3%) on faster-growing attritional lines such as Crop and Casualty. The new term loan and acquisition intangibles add interest and amortization. Nine-month GAAP annualized ROE of 22.3% is still high, but the trend is down from the 2025 peak.
situation.why: 2025 was a benign catastrophe year and the highest-return year in the record, so it overstates a normal return. Premium growth of about 32% needs capital, and the company has added a $294 million term loan and absorbed an unrealized bond loss in equity. Even so, it is paying dividends and repurchasing shares, which suggests capital is not binding today, though the evidence does not show subsidiary statutory surplus or ratings headroom.

book_growth.why: Year 1 growth is held down by a $63.8M unrealized loss on available-for-sale bonds, $73.0M of buybacks and the new dividend, even though earnings are strong. Later years return to about 10-12% as earnings retention exceeds payouts. Growth is high because ROE is high and about 40% of income is paid out.

quotes.quote: Our current reinsurance program limits our pre-tax net loss from any single event to $20.0 million for earthquakes and $11.0 million for hurricanes

fade_years.why: Moving from the current 17-20% ROE and 10% growth to mid-teens ROE and 3.5% growth takes a long fade. 10 years reflects a franchise with some competitive edge that is gradually competed away.

quotes.quote: Total loss ratio of 41.5% compared to 32.3% in the third quarter of 2025

long_run_roe.why: The company has a differentiated, analytics-led franchise, but long-run catastrophe loads, competition and new debt and intangibles should push ROE toward mid-teens. That is still above the 9.3% cost of equity. The loss ratio is already rising, which supports fading.

quotes.quote: For the full year 2026, the Company expects to achieve adjusted net income of $280 million to $285 million. This includes an estimate of $8 million to $12 million of catastrophe losses for the year.

roe.why: Nine-month 2026 net income of $160.9M and guidance for adjusted net income of $280-285M imply year-1 GAAP ROE of about 23% on the opening $942.7M. After that I fade ROE as catastrophe losses normalise from a very low base, attritional losses rise and interest costs run for a full year.

terminal_growth.why: Long-run book growth should converge close to the nominal anchor of 3.75%, slightly below it given a maturing premium base. The company is still growing premiums at 28-32%, which supports staying near the anchor rather than far below it.

risks.risk: A severe catastrophe or reserve shortfall, or a continued rise in attritional losses, would cut ROE sharply. Catastrophe losses are currently very low.
The long-run ROE falls to a normal specialty-insurer level as the catastrophe load normalises, competition rises and acquisition debt and intangibles weigh.
Growth is slower because a reinsurance or capital limit, a rating issue, or a further AOCI loss restricts how fast equity can grow.

situation.roe_position: ROE is high because Palomar is a fast-growing specialty P&C insurer with a low combined ratio, heavy reinsurance and modest catastrophe losses. 2025 catastrophe losses were slightly negative. 2026 catastrophe losses are guided to only $8-12 million. Attritional losses are rising with the shift to Crop and Casualty, and new acquisition debt adds interest cost, so ROE should drift down from the 27% peak as catastrophe loads normalise.
situation.why: The 2025 ROE of 27% rests on benign catastrophe experience, a falling expense ratio and a rapidly growing book. Growth of about 30% in written premium draws on capital, and equity is cut by AOCI losses, buybacks and a new dividend. The filings show no statutory capital ratios or dividend limits, so the constraint cannot be judged. The company has in effect chosen to return capital while using debt to fund acquisitions.

flags: Palomar completed its acquisition of Gray Surety, a Treasury-listed surety carrier, and renamed it Palomar Casualty & Surety Company (PCSC).
To fund the Gray Surety acquisition, Palomar entered into a credit agreement for unsecured credit facilities. The nine-month cash flow statement shows term loan proceeds.
In its third-quarter results release, Palomar gave full-year adjusted net income guidance of $280 million to $285 million. The CEO described this as the fourth increase to that guidance range.
